head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dijkstra's algorithm: always expand the room reachable earliest (min-heap, a priority queue)
Move costs alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, … by the parity of the cell you leave from
Cost depends on the position (checkerboard parity)
You may enter the neighbour only at or after its opening time moveTime, so wait if needed, then pay the move cost

bullets: Time to reach the last room: 7.

blocks.h: Why Dijkstra and not BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
p: Edges have different costs (1 or 2) and arrival also depends on opening times, so plain BFS layers do not give the earliest time. Dijkstra's algorithm correctly handles it because waiting never makes a later arrival better (arrival times are monotone).

3342.takeaway: Dijkstra over rooms: new time = max(current time, room opening time) + a move cost that alternates 1 and 2 by cell parity.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum sum of nums[i:] with `a` halving operations and `b` subtract-k operations still available
Memoized DP (Dynamic Programming) over (index, operations left)
Operation 2: subtract k, only allowed if x ≥ k
If both are applied to the same number the order matters: subtract then halve → (x − k + 1) // 2; halve then subtract → ceil(x / 2) − k (needs ceil(x/2) ≥ k); take the better

p: `nums = [2,8,3,19,3]`, `k = 3`, `op1 = 1`, `op2 = 1`. Options for each number when used (halve / subtract):
bullets: The search returns 23: spend the halving on 19 (→ 10) and the subtraction on 8 (→ 5): 2 + 5 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 23.

blocks.h: Why a DP and not a greedy?
p: The two operations interact: applying both to one number can beat applying each to a different one, and the best number for each operation depends on the other. Trying every choice per index with memoization is exact, in O(n · op1 · op2) states.

3366.takeaway: Memoized DP over (index, halvings left, subtractions left), trying none / one / both operations on each element.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A subarray (i, j] has length divisible by k iff i and j have the same remainder mod k
The smallest prefix sum seen at an index with remainder r (index 0 counts with prefix 0)
Largest subarray sum ending at j with length divisible by k
The prefix for the current j is added after computing, so a subarray never has length 0

blocks.h: Why the smallest prefix per remainder?
p: For a fixed right end j, the subarray sum is pre[j] − pre[i] over earlier i with the same remainder; it is largest when pre[i] is smallest. Keeping the minimum per remainder class is enough.

3381.takeaway: Prefix sums grouped by index remainder mod k; subtract the smallest earlier prefix of the same remainder.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A rate a→b = r also gives b→a = 1/r: edges in both directions
val = {initial: 1.0}; DFS (Depth-First Search) with a stack
val[c] = how many units of c one unit of the start currency becomes on that day (a path product; consistent for any path because rates are consistent)
Propagating a ratio from a root
Day 1 turns 1 unit into r1[c] units of c; day 2, one unit of the start currency would give r2[c] units of c, so the day-2 conversion from c back to the start gives 1 / r2[c] per unit
Convert forth on day 1 and back on day 2
max(... for c in r1 if c in r2)
Pick the best intermediate currency c reachable on both days

p: Start with EUR. Day 1: EUR→USD 2, USD→JPY 3. Day 2: JPY→USD 4, USD→CHF 5, CHF→EUR 6.
bullets: Best: 720.0 EUR (convert to JPY on day 1).

p: On day 2 the graph's rates describe how much of c one EUR buys (r2[c]). Going from c to EUR on day 2 therefore multiplies by 1 / r2[c], and the total is r1[c] / r2[c]. Every currency in both graphs is a candidate for the overnight holding.

3387.takeaway: Compute per-day currency ratios from the start, then maximise r1[c] / r2[c] over currencies c present on both days.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Smallest L such that every run of identical characters can be shortened to at most L using at most numOps flips; feasibility is monotone in L
From `itertools`: yields each run of identical characters
A run of length r needs floor(r / (L + 1)) flips to break it into pieces of length ≤ L (flip every (L+1)-th character)
Runs must all have length 1, i.e. the string must alternate; count mismatches with 0101… and with 1010… and take the cheaper
The special case: flips of a run can merge with neighbours when L = 1

p: For L ≥ 2, flipping the middle of a long run does not merge it with a neighbouring run into something longer than L. For L = 1 the flips change the neighbours' runs too, so the problem becomes making the whole string alternating, which has just two target patterns.

bullets: Space: O(1) beyond the run iterator.

3399.takeaway: Binary search on the longest allowed run L; each run costs floor(len / (L+1)) flips, and L = 1 means making the string alternate.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The value of the cell above after any increments
Increments needed so this cell is strictly greater than the one above
The new value of this cell becomes the cell above for the next row

p: The condition is only about vertical neighbours, so each column can be processed separately. Greedy: raise each cell only as much as needed, since a larger value would force bigger increments below.

3402.takeaway: Per column, raise each cell to just above the one before it and sum the increments.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Choose which k of the n − 1 adjacent pairs are equal (`math.comb`, binomial coefficient)
The first element can be anything: m choices
Each of the other n − 1 − k adjacent pairs must differ, so the next element has m − 1 choices; modular exponentiation

p: Fix which adjacent pairs are equal (C(n−1, k) ways). Then walk left to right: the first element has m choices, an 'equal' pair gives 1 choice, and a 'different' pair gives m − 1 choices. The choices are independent, so they multiply.

bullets: Time: O(n) for comb, O(log n) for pow.

3405.takeaway: Closed form: C(n−1, k) · m · (m−1)^(n−1−k), mod 10⁹+7.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The CURRENT truth about each live task
Max-heap by priority, then by task id, using negated values in Python's min-heap; every edit pushes a new entry and leaves the old one
Just forgets the task; its heap entries become stale
An entry is valid only if the task is still live AND its priority equals the stored one; stale entries are discarded

p: A binary heap cannot remove or change an arbitrary entry in O(log n). Pushing the new version and ignoring outdated versions on pop keeps every operation O(log n) amortized.

3408.takeaway: Dict of live tasks plus a max-heap with lazy deletion of stale (outdated) entries.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each digit appears in the whole string
The two adjacent digits must be different
A digit is valid if it appears exactly as many times as its own value
Scans left to right, so the first match is returned

p: The validity of a digit depends on its count in the WHOLE string, not just near the pair. One pass builds all counts, then a second pass finds the first adjacent pair that satisfies the rule.

3438.takeaway: Count all digits first, then scan adjacent pairs for different digits whose counts equal their values.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost to fix positions i+1.. (the rest of the caption) given that position i holds letter c in a run of current length k (k = 3 means 'at least 3')
DP (Dynamic Programming) from the right with a run-length state capped at 3
Cost of changing a letter to c: the distance in the alphabet (each step to the next or previous letter is one operation)
Continue the same letter: the run grows (capped at 3)
k == 3: switch to d ≠ c with run 1
A run may only end once it has length ≥ 3, so changing to another letter is allowed only from k = 3
Good caption = every run has length ≥ 3
After computing the minimum total, walks forward picking, at each position, the SMALLEST letter that still achieves the remaining cost: this gives the lexicographically smallest caption
Rebuilding the answer from a DP table

p: `caption = "cdcd"`:
bullets: A caption is good when every run of equal letters has length ≥ 3. For length 4 that forces one single run, so all letters must become the same; the cheapest, lexicographically smallest choice is `cccc` (cost 2).

blocks.h: Why track run length only up to 3?
p: Once a run has reached length 3 it is allowed to end, and longer runs behave identically. So states 1, 2 and 3 (meaning 3 or more) capture everything the future needs.

3441.takeaway: Right-to-left DP over (position, letter, run length capped at 3), then a forward pass choosing the smallest letter that keeps the optimum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The four diagonal directions in clockwise order; turning right by 90° means d → (d + 1) % 4
Longest valid segment starting at (i, j), moving in direction d, with a flag for whether the single allowed clockwise turn was used
Memoized DFS (Depth-First Search) with a small state
The sequence must go 1, 2, 0, 2, 0, …: after a 2 comes 0, after a 0 (or the starting 1) comes 2
At any cell you may turn once, then continue straight

p: 5×5 grid from the problem. Start cells (value 1) and directions with a segment longer than 1:
Only one turn is allowed, so the state is just 'not yet turned' or 'already turned'. Together with the position and direction that gives 4·2 states per cell, so memoization keeps it O(m·n).

3459.takeaway: Memoized DFS along diagonals: pattern 1,2,0,2,0…, at most one clockwise turn.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The result has n + m − 1 characters; None means 'not decided yet'
for 'T' at i: write str2 at i..i+m−1
Each 'T' forces the window to equal str2; conflicting forced letters mean the answer is the empty string
Remember which positions are fixed by 'T'
for 'F' where the window equals str2
A forbidden match appeared: change the LAST non-forced position of that window to 'b' (the rightmost position changes the string least), or fail if every position is forced
Greedy repair that keeps lexicographic order

p: `str1 = "TFTF"`, `str2 = "ab"`: the string has 5 characters. After forcing T windows (positions 0–1 and 2–3 are `ab`) and filling with `a`, the F windows are checked:

head: step
rows: F window at 1 is 'ba', not 'ab': fine
F window at 3 is 'ba', not 'ab': fine

blocks.h: Why change the rightmost free position?
p: Changing an earlier letter would make the string lexicographically larger at an earlier index. Changing the rightmost unforced position of the offending window to 'b' (the next smallest letter after 'a') raises the string as late as possible. The change might create a new match in a later window, but later windows are checked afterwards in the same pass.

3474.takeaway: Force T windows to str2, fill free positions with 'a', then repair F windows that still equal str2 by bumping their rightmost free position to 'b'.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Which baskets already hold a fruit
Scan baskets left to right: the problem requires the leftmost suitable basket
The `else` of a `for` runs only if the loop finished without `break`, i.e. no basket was found
Counts fruits that found no basket

p: The rule is exactly 'leftmost available basket with enough capacity', so following it directly is O(n²), fine for n ≤ 100. A segment tree over the baskets' capacities speeds the 'leftmost with capacity ≥ f' query to O(log n) for larger inputs.

3477.takeaway: First-fit simulation with for/else counting fruits that find no basket.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: For each conflicting pair (a < b), remember it at its right end b
The largest and second-largest left endpoints among pairs with right end ≤ r
Number of valid subarrays ending at r: start must be greater than top1 (the closest conflicting left endpoint that blocks)
If the pair giving top1 were removed, starts could extend left down to top2 + 1: the gain credited to that pair (identified by its left endpoint top1)
Credit assignment to the blocking pair
Best choice of one pair to remove

bullets: Total without removals: 6; best removal adds 3; answer 9.

p: At each r only the strongest blocker (largest left endpoint, top1) restricts the starts. Removing that pair makes the next strongest (top2) the restriction, adding top1 − top2 valid starts. Pairs that never are the strongest blocker give no gain, so they need not be tracked.

3480.takeaway: Sweep right ends keeping the two largest left endpoints; removing the pair behind top1 gains top1 − top2 starts at every r where it dominates.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The array is not yet non-decreasing
Index of the adjacent pair with the smallest sum; `min` returns the FIRST such index on ties, which is the required leftmost pair
Slice assignment replacing two items by their sum

p: The rule fixes which pair to merge (smallest sum, leftmost on ties), so the process is deterministic. Each iteration is O(n) and there are at most n merges: O(n²), fine for n ≤ 50.

3507.takeaway: Simulate: repeatedly merge the leftmost adjacent pair with the smallest sum until the array is sorted.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Indexes already executed: visiting one again would loop forever, so stop
Stop when the pointer leaves the array
Add and move to the next instruction
Move by the given offset (may be negative)

p: Instructions `jump, add, add, jump, add, jump`, values `[2,1,3,1,-2,-3]`:
Jumps can send you back to an instruction already executed, which would repeat forever. Remembering visited indexes ends the program when a cycle appears.

3522.takeaway: Simulate with a visited set: stop when the index leaves the array or repeats.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Directed tree: one unit of type a equals f units of type b
Units of v per unit of type 0 = (units of u per unit of 0) × f, modulo 10⁹+7
Visits each node after its parent, so res[u] is ready when needed

p: `[[0,1,2],[1,2,3]]`: 1 unit of type 0 is 2 of type 1, and 1 of type 1 is 3 of type 2.

blocks.h: Why no cycles to worry about?
p: There are n − 1 conversions forming a tree rooted at type 0, so every type is reached exactly once and no visited set is needed.

3528.takeaway: BFS down the conversion tree, multiplying the factor along each edge (mod 10⁹+7).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: F, B (prefix sums over the doubled arrays)
F[i] = total forward travel time to pass i houses; B similar for backward. Doubling the array handles wrap-around on a circle
f = F[q or q + n] − F[cur]
Forward time from house cur to house q (going around if q is behind)
Backward time from cur to q, using the backward edge costs
Take the cheaper direction for each query

p: `forward = [1,4,4]`, `backward = [4,1,2]`, start at house 0, visit queries `[1,2,0,2]` in order:
Going around a circle past the end needs sums that wrap. Extending the arrays to length 2n lets every range sum be a difference of two prefix values without special cases.

3540.takeaway: Circular travel with doubled prefix-sum arrays; each query takes the cheaper of the forward and backward routes.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: All cells carrying each portal letter
Teleporting costs 0, so those cells go to the FRONT of the double-ended queue (deque), keeping distances in order
A normal move costs 1: add to the back
A portal letter is used at most once, since after the first use all its cells are already reached at that distance

p: Edges have weight 0 (teleports) or 1 (steps). A deque keeps the queue ordered by distance: 0-cost neighbours go to the front, 1-cost ones to the back, giving Dijkstra's answer in O(V + E).

3552.takeaway: 0-1 BFS: portals teleport at cost 0 (pushed to the front), steps cost 1 (back); each letter is used once.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Each group of three uses three elements
The second-largest remaining element: take the largest as the 'high', the next as the median, and discard a small one

p: Sorted `[1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]`, 2 groups:

Each group's median is the middle value of three elements. To make medians large, each group should use one very large element, one large median, and the smallest remaining as the low element. Taking, from the top, a pair (largest, second largest) and the smallest leftover gives the best medians: the second largest, fourth largest, and so on.

3627.takeaway: Sort; the best medians are the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … largest values (one group per three elements).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Splits the array into about √n blocks of size √n (sqrt decomposition)
Range queries with precomputation per block range
Sorted positions of every value, so a value's frequency in [l, r] is two binary searches: bisect_right(pos, r) − bisect_left(pos, l)
Precomputed most frequent value (smallest value on ties, via the key (count, −value)) in whole blocks bi..bj
Table of answers for block ranges
The majority-like value of a query is either the mode of the full blocks inside, or occurs in the partial blocks at the ends, so only those values need testing
Highest frequency, ties broken toward the smaller value

p: Counting each query by scanning costs O(n) per query. Precomputing the mode for every block range costs O(n √n) in total, and each query then tests O(√n) candidates, each with an O(log n) frequency lookup.

3636.takeaway: Square-root decomposition: precomputed block-range modes plus end-block candidates, with bisect for exact frequencies.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A sensor covers a (2k + 1) × (2k + 1) square around it
Ceiling division: how many squares of that side fit along n
Sensors needed across rows times across columns

p: Each sensor covers at most one square of side 2k+1, and the squares can be placed without overlap to cover the whole grid, so the minimum is the number of tiles needed along each axis, multiplied.

3648.takeaway: Tile the grid with (2k+1)×(2k+1) squares: ceil(n/side) × ceil(m/side).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Grid DP (Dynamic Programming): min cost to each cell moving only right/down, where seed[i][j] is an alternative starting cost (arriving by teleport); cost of a cell is paid on entering it
Layered DP, one layer per teleport
at[v] = min dp over cells with value v
Cheapest way to stand on any cell of value v
Cheapest cost among cells with value ≥ v: a teleport goes from a cell to any cell whose value is ≤ the source, so a target of value w can be reached from any source with value ≥ w
Next layer: arrive at any cell by teleport at the suffix cost (teleport is free), or by walking
Allows up to k teleports, one layer each

p: `grid = [[1,3,3],[2,5,4],[4,3,5]]`, `k = 2`: cost to reach the bottom-right with more teleports allowed:

head: teleports allowed
min cost to reach the end

p: A teleport from cell u to cell v is allowed if grid[v] ≤ grid[u]. For each target value w, the best source is the cheapest cell with value ≥ w, which a suffix minimum over values sorted in descending order provides in O(1) after one pass.

bullets: Time: O(k · (m·n + V log V)) for V distinct values.

3651.takeaway: Layered grid DP: each teleport layer seeds every cell with the suffix-minimum cost over cells of larger or equal value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Current priority of every live event
Min-heap with negated priority: the highest priority comes first, and among equal priorities the SMALLER id (as the tuple sorts ascending)
Max-heap via negation, tie-break by id
Builds the heap from the initial list in O(n)
The old entry stays in the heap as a stale entry
An entry is valid only if cur[eid] equals its priority; valid ones are removed from the dict and returned

p: Changing the priority of an arbitrary heap entry is not supported. Pushing a fresh entry and discarding stale ones on pop keeps updates O(log n) and each stale entry is popped at most once.

bullets: Time: O(log n) amortized per operation.

3885.takeaway: Max-heap with lazy deletion: keep current priorities in a dict and discard heap entries that no longer match.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Increase needed so nums[i] is strictly greater than both neighbours: max(0, max(neighbours) + 1 − nums[i])
Making an index a local peak
With an odd length the maximum number of special (peak) indexes is (n − 1)/2 and the only way is every second index

With an even length one gap in the alternation is allowed: the first j peaks sit at odd positions from the left and the remaining peaks at positions counted from the right; the minimum over where the shift happens
Prefix and suffix sums combined at a split point

p: `nums = [2,1,1,3]` (n = 4, even): costs of the left- and right-aligned options at each split:

blocks.h: Why a split for even n?
p: To get the maximum count of peaks in an even-length array you can place peaks at odd indexes up to some point and then shift the pattern by one. Prefix sums for the left part and suffix sums for the right part give the cost of each split in O(1), and the best split is found in one pass.

3891.takeaway: Cost to make an index a peak; odd n sums fixed positions, even n minimises over a split of left- and right-aligned peaks.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Best sum of an alternating subsequence ending at i where nums[i] is a high point (peak) / low point (valley)
j = i − k; add j to the trees
Only elements at distance ≥ k are eligible predecessors, so element i − k is inserted into the structures when i reaches it
Delayed insertion for a distance constraint
A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) for prefix MAXIMUM: best valley[j] among eligible j with a smaller value, because a peak must come after a valley of smaller value
The same trick with reversed ranks: best peak[j] among eligible j with a larger value, for a valley
Suffix max as a prefix max
Start a new subsequence (0) or extend the best compatible one

blocks.h: Why Fenwick trees with delayed insertion?
p: The inner question is 'max over eligible earlier elements whose value is below / above nums[i]', a range maximum over values. A Fenwick tree stores maxima by value rank and answers in O(log n). The distance rule is handled by inserting element i − k only when i is reached.

3915.takeaway: Two-state DP (peak / valley) with Fenwick trees for prefix maxima over value ranks; elements enter the trees k steps late.
